summary.text: A rustic culture-god, son of Apollo by the nymph Cyrene (`cyrene-nymph`), whom the corn-rich Haemonians call 'Hunter' and 'Shepherd'; reared in Cheiron's cave, he was taught healing and prophecy by the Muses and made keeper of their flocks.
He married Autonoe, daughter of Cadmus, binding the bee-keeper's craft into the royal house of Thebes.

story.text: Apollo carried Cyrene (`cyrene-nymph`) off far from Haemonia and set her among the nymphs of Libya by the Myrtosian height, where she bore him Aristaeus, whom the corn-rich Haemonians call 'Hunter' and 'Shepherd'. The god brought his son while still an infant to be nurtured in the cave of Cheiron, and when he grew to manhood the Muses gave him a bride, taught him the arts of healing and of prophecy, and made him the keeper of their sheep.
He is the lord of honey, who discovered the works of bees and the fatness of the olive, the fruit of labour; the rustic crafts of herd, hive, and cheese are his gift to mortals.

Hyginus lists him among the Sons of Apollo, the last entry of the catalogue: 'Aristaeus by Cyrene, daughter of Peneus' — the Libyan nymph now entered as `cyrene-nymph`, distinct from Cyrene consort of Ares in the Thracian labour.

Long-haired Aristaeus wedded Autonoe, daughter of Cadmus and Harmonia, and to them was born a son, Actaeon, who was bred by Chiron to be a hunter and afterwards devoured on Cithaeron by his own dogs. The sources quarrel over the cause: according to Acusilaus, whom Apollodorus cites, Zeus was angry at him for wooing Semele; but the version Hyginus tells has him punished by Artemis for seeing the goddess bathe, and on the painting at Delphi Pausanias saw him set beside his mother, a young deer in their hands and a hound stretched at their side.

Hyginus gives the common cause of Actaeon's ruin: the shepherd, son of Aristaeus and Autonoe, saw Diana bathing and desired her, and in anger the goddess set horns upon his head so that his own dogs tore him apart; the same end is shown on the Delphic painting Pausanias describes, where Actaeon sits with his mother, a fawn and a hunting dog beside them.
Deeply grieved by the fate of Actaeon, and vexed alike with Boeotia and the whole of Greece, Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, is said to have migrated from the land to Sardinia.

When Sirius scorched the Minoan isles and no respite came to their inhabitants, the Far-Darter's oracle summoned Aristaeus to ward off the pestilence. At his father Apollo's command he left Phthia and made his home in Ceos, gathered the Parrhasian people who are of the lineage of Lycaon, and built a great altar to Zeus Icmaeus; upon the mountains he offered sacrifice to that star and to Zeus son of Cronus — and from that rite, Apollonius says, the Etesian winds cool the land for forty days, and on Ceos even in later times the priests still perform the same observances.

Hyginus preserves a Ceian variant: when Icarus' murderers hid among the islanders and Canicula brought plague, Aristaeus son of Apollo and Cyrene asked his father how to free the state. Apollo bade them expiate Icarus' death with many victims and pray Jove for wind when the Dog-star rises — and Aristaeus obtained the Etesian breeze that tempers Canicula's heat.
Pausanias counts Aristaeus among those mortals who in ancient days were changed to gods and still receive honours — alongside Britomartis, Heracles, Amphiaraus, and the Dioscuri.
